claim: Hair cells detect sounds by transducing mechanical vibrations into electrical signals.
source: Hair cells, the receptors of the inner ear, detect sounds by transducing mechanical vibrations into electrical signals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in auditory neuroscience, presented as background information in the abstract.

claim: The hair bundle is a mechanical antenna that protrudes from the top surface of each hair cell.
source: From the top surface of each hair cell protrudes a mechanical antenna, the hair bundle, which the cell uses to detect and amplify auditory stimuli, thus sharpening frequency selectivity and providing a broad dynamic range.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell structure and function.

claim: The hair bundle is used to detect and amplify auditory stimuli.
source: From the top surface of each hair cell protrudes a mechanical antenna, the hair bundle, which the cell uses to detect and amplify auditory stimuli, thus sharpening frequency selectivity and providing a broad dynamic range.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle function.

claim: The hair bundle sharpens frequency selectivity.
source: From the top surface of each hair cell protrudes a mechanical antenna, the hair bundle, which the cell uses to detect and amplify auditory stimuli, thus sharpening frequency selectivity and providing a broad dynamic range.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle function.

claim: The hair bundle provides a broad dynamic range.
source: From the top surface of each hair cell protrudes a mechanical antenna, the hair bundle, which the cell uses to detect and amplify auditory stimuli, thus sharpening frequency selectivity and providing a broad dynamic range.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle function.

claim: Current methods for mechanically stimulating hair bundles are too slow to encompass the frequency range of mammalian hearing.
source: Current methods for mechanically stimulating hair bundles are too slow to encompass the frequency range of mammalian hearing and are plagued by inconsistencies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing methods, which is elaborated in the Introduction section.

claim: Current methods for mechanically stimulating hair bundles are plagued by inconsistencies.
source: Current methods for mechanically stimulating hair bundles are too slow to encompass the frequency range of mammalian hearing and are plagued by inconsistencies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing methods, which is elaborated in the Introduction section.

claim: The authors have developed a method to move individual hair bundles with photonic force.
source: To overcome these challenges, we have developed a method to move individual hair bundles with photonic force.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The photonic force technique uses an optical fiber whose tip is tapered to a diameter of a few micrometers.
source: This technique uses an optical fiber whose tip is tapered to a diameter of a few micrometers and endowed with a ball lens to minimize divergence of the light beam.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed, supported by fabrication details in Materials and methods.

claim: The optical fiber tip is endowed with a ball lens to minimize divergence of the light beam.
source: This technique uses an optical fiber whose tip is tapered to a diameter of a few micrometers and endowed with a ball lens to minimize divergence of the light beam.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed, supported by fabrication details in Materials and methods.

claim: The authors demonstrate the rapid application of photonic force to vestibular and cochlear hair cells.
source: Here we describe the fabrication, characterization, and application of this optical system and demonstrate the rapid application of photonic force to vestibular and cochlear hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing responses of hair bundles from bullfrog sacculus and rat cochlea.

claim: Hair cells in the auditory and vestibular systems of vertebrates convert mechanical stimuli into electrical signals through mechanoelectrical transduction.
source: Hair cells in the auditory and vestibular systems of vertebrates convert mechanical stimuli into electrical signals through the process of mechanoelectrical transduction (Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Martin and Hudspeth, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hair bundle is a cluster of stereocilia.
source: The mechanical receptor for such stimuli is the hair bundle, a cluster of stereocilia, or stiff enlarged microvilli, atop each hair cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle structure.

claim: Stereocilia are stiff enlarged microvilli.
source: The mechanical receptor for such stimuli is the hair bundle, a cluster of stereocilia, or stiff enlarged microvilli, atop each hair cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereocilia structure.

claim: The tip link is an extracellular molecular filament that extends from the tip of each stereocilium to the side of its tallest neighbor.
source: An extracellular molecular filament, the tip link, extends from the tip of each stereocilium to the side of its tallest neighbor in the plane parallel to the bundle's axis of symmetry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle structure.

claim: Mechanically gated ion channels are located at the lower end of each tip link.
source: Mechanically gated ion channels are located at the lower end of each tip link.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of transduction channels.

claim: When a hair bundle pivots toward its tall edge, the increased tension in the tip links opens the ion channels.
source: When a hair bundle pivots at its base toward its tall edge in response to stimulation, the increased tension in the tip links opens the ion channels and the ensuing ionic current depolarizes the cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mechanoelectrical transduction, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The ionic current resulting from channel opening depolarizes the hair cell.
source: When a hair bundle pivots at its base toward its tall edge in response to stimulation, the increased tension in the tip links opens the ion channels and the ensuing ionic current depolarizes the cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mechanoelectrical transduction, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: One method to apply force to a hair bundle is to deflect it with a compliant glass fiber about 100 μm in length and 1 μm in diameter.
source: The first is to deflect the bundle with a compliant glass fiber about 100 μm in length and 1 nm in diameter (Crawford and Fettiplace, 1985; Howard and Ashmore, 1986; Howard and Hudspeth, 1988).
evidence: This describes an existing method, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The glass fiber used to deflect hair bundles is subjected to hydrodynamic drag that roughly doubles that on the bundle.
source: Because the preparation is immersed in an aqueous solution, however, the fiber is subjected to hydrodynamic drag that roughly doubles that on the bundle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of the system.

claim: For a typical fiber of stiffness 500 μN•m–1 and drag coefficient 150 nN•s•m–1, the time constant of responsiveness is about 300 μs.
source: For a typical fiber of stiffness 500 μN•m–1 and drag coefficient 150 nN•s•m–1, the time constant of responsiveness is about 300 μs, which corresponds to a low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency near 500 Hz (Crawford and Fettiplace, 1985; Howard and Hudspeth, 1987).
evidence: This is a calculation based on physical parameters, supported by citations.

claim: A time constant of 300 μs corresponds to a low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency near 500 Hz.
source: For a typical fiber of stiffness 500 μN•m–1 and drag coefficient 150 nN•s•m–1, the time constant of responsiveness is about 300 μs, which corresponds to a low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency near 500 Hz (Crawford and Fettiplace, 1985; Howard and Hudspeth, 1987).
evidence: This is a calculation based on physical parameters, supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian hair bundle stereocilia are less cohesive than those of amphibians.
source: Another problem is especially acute for the stimulation of mammalian hair bundles, whose stereocilia are less cohesive than those of amphibians: when a fiber is attached at a single site in the hair bundle, the displacement of other stereocilia depends in a complex manner on elastic and hydrodynamic coupling across the bundle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between mammalian and amphibian hair bundles.

claim: When a fiber is attached at a single site in a mammalian hair bundle, the displacement of other stereocilia depends in a complex manner on elastic and hydrodynamic coupling across the bundle.
source: Another problem is especially acute for the stimulation of mammalian hair bundles, whose stereocilia are less cohesive than those of amphibians: when a fiber is attached at a single site in the hair bundle, the displacement of other stereocilia depends in a complex manner on elastic and hydrodynamic coupling across the bundle.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanical behavior of mammalian hair bundles.

claim: Single-site attachment of a fiber to a mammalian hair bundle results in uneven application of force to different stereocilia and can produce artifacts.
source: This arrangement results in an uneven application of force to different stereocilia and can produce artifacts (Indzhykulian et al., 2013; Nam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work documenting these artifacts.

claim: The second common method of stimulation uses a fluid jet that displaces a hair bundle through the action of a piezoelectric diaphragm.
source: The second common method of stimulation uses a fluid jet that displaces a hair bundle through the action of a piezoelectric diaphragm (Géléoc et al., 1997; Corns et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes an existing method, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The resonant frequency of fluid injection can reach 5 kHz.
source: Although the resonant frequency of fluid injection can reach 5 kHz, practical use of the method is limited to less than 1 kHz owing to uncertainties in force calibration (Dinklo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Practical use of the fluid jet method is limited to less than 1 kHz owing to uncertainties in force calibration.
source: Although the resonant frequency of fluid injection can reach 5 kHz, practical use of the method is limited to less than 1 kHz owing to uncertainties in force calibration (Dinklo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fluid leakage from the fluid jet system might introduce a displacement bias.
source: Moreover, fluid leakage from the system might introduce a displacement bias.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential problem with the fluid jet method.

claim: The inability of current methods to reach higher frequencies by direct stimulation limits quantitative understanding of hair-cell mechanics over more than 95% of the range of mammalian hearing.
source: In summary, the inability of current methods to reach higher frequencies by direct stimulation limits our quantitative understanding of hair-cell mechanics over more than 95% of the range of mammalian hearing, which extends to 20 kHz in humans and at least 150 kHz in some species of bats and whales.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency limitations of current methods and the range of mammalian hearing.

claim: Mammalian hearing extends to 20 kHz in humans.
source: In summary, the inability of current methods to reach higher frequencies by direct stimulation limits our quantitative understanding of hair-cell mechanics over more than 95% of the range of mammalian hearing, which extends to 20 kHz in humans and at least 150 kHz in some species of bats and whales.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the range of human hearing.

claim: Mammalian hearing extends to at least 150 kHz in some species of bats and whales.
source: In summary, the inability of current methods to reach higher frequencies by direct stimulation limits our quantitative understanding of hair-cell mechanics over more than 95% of the range of mammalian hearing, which extends to 20 kHz in humans and at least 150 kHz in some species of bats and whales.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the range of hearing in some mammals.

claim: The susceptibility of current approaches to artifacts has long impeded understanding of hearing, particularly in the mammalian ear.
source: What is more, the susceptibility of current approaches to artifacts has long impeded our understanding of hearing, in particular in the case of the mammalian ear (Nam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Photonic force arises when photons are absorbed, reflected, or refracted upon interaction with an object.
source: Because photonic force arises when photons are absorbed, reflected, or refracted upon interaction with an object, intense illumination should apply substantial force to a bundle.
evidence: This is established knowledge from physics.

claim: Intense illumination should apply substantial force to a hair bundle.
source: Because photonic force arises when photons are absorbed, reflected, or refracted upon interaction with an object, intense illumination should apply substantial force to a bundle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of photonic force.

claim: The experiments confirmed the validity of the photonic force approach.
source: Our experiments confirmed the validity of the approach and demonstrated that the requisite irradiation does not jeopardize a bundle's operation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The requisite irradiation does not jeopardize a bundle's operation.
source: Our experiments confirmed the validity of the approach and demonstrated that the requisite irradiation does not jeopardize a bundle's operation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing preserved spontaneous oscillations after irradiation.

claim: The photonic force method allows probing of hair-bundle physiology at previously inaccessible timescales.
source: This method allows us to probe hair-bundle physiology at previously inaccessible timescales, for the delivery time of the stimulus can accommodate the full frequency range of mammalian hearing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rapid responses with time constants of a few hundred microseconds.

claim: The delivery time of the photonic force stimulus can accommodate the full frequency range of mammalian hearing.
source: This method allows us to probe hair-bundle physiology at previously inaccessible timescales, for the delivery time of the stimulus can accommodate the full frequency range of mammalian hearing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid response times observed in the experiments.

claim: The photonic force approach avoids the artifacts that bedevil current methods.
source: At the same time, this approach avoids the artifacts that bedevil current methods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uniform illumination of stereocilia and the absence of mechanical attachment.

claim: Reflected, absorbed, and refracted photons exert force on a target.
source: The conservation of momentum entails that reflected, absorbed, and refracted photons exert force on a target.
evidence: This is established knowledge from physics.

claim: All three phenomena (reflection, absorption, refraction) are likely to take place when light strikes an array of stereocilia in a hair bundle.
source: All these phenomena are likely to take place when light strikes an array of stereocilia in a hair bundle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optical properties of stereocilia.

claim: Multiple modes of light propagation occur in a hair bundle by virtue of the cylindrical shape of the stereocilia.
source: Although an analysis based on reflection alone would indicate that a hair bundle is relatively insensitive to radiation pressure, geometric considerations reveal that multiple modes of light propagation occur in a hair bundle by virtue of the cylindrical shape of the stereocilia (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference based on geometric optics, detailed in Materials and methods.

claim: Each mode of light propagation is capable of transferring momentum and mechanically stimulating the bundle.
source: Each of these modes is capable of transferring momentum and therefore of mechanically stimulating the bundle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of momentum transfer.

claim: The diameter of each stereocilium compares to the wavelength of light.
source: Because the diameter of each stereocilium compares to the wavelength of light, the regular spacing of stereocilia within the hair bundle might additionally give rise to complex interference effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereocilium dimensions and light wavelengths.

claim: The regular spacing of stereocilia within the hair bundle might give rise to complex interference effects.
source: Because the diameter of each stereocilium compares to the wavelength of light, the regular spacing of stereocilia within the hair bundle might additionally give rise to complex interference effects.
evidence: This is speculation about potential optical effects.

claim: The core of an intact optical fiber is only 5 μm in diameter.
source: Even after the jacket has been removed, the core of the fiber—which is only 5 μm in diameter—lies within a cylinder of glass cladding about 125 μm across.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical fiber used.

claim: The core of an optical fiber lies within a cylinder of glass cladding about 125 μm across.
source: Even after the jacket has been removed, the core of the fiber—which is only 5 μm in diameter—lies within a cylinder of glass cladding about 125 μm across.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical fiber used.

claim: It was necessary to strip the jacket and taper the cladding to bring the fiber's core near a hair bundle without impingement.
source: In order to bring the fiber's core near a hair bundle without impingement of the fiber's outer layers on the experimental preparation, it was necessary to strip the jacket and taper the cladding.
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication process developed by the authors.

claim: By melting the tip of the fiber's core, a hemispherical lens with a divergence angle in water of approximately 11° was created.
source: By melting the tip of the fiber's core, we created a hemispherical lens with a divergence angle in water of approximately 11° (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication process and its result.

claim: Hair bundles in the bullfrog's sacculus are about 8 μm tall.
source: This objective could be achieved readily for a flat sensory epithelium such as that of the bullfrog's sacculus, in which the bundles are about 8 μm tall and are separated by approximately 15 μm (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bullfrog saccular hair bundles.

claim: Hair bundles in the bullfrog's sacculus are separated by approximately 15 μm.
source: This objective could be achieved readily for a flat sensory epithelium such as that of the bullfrog's sacculus, in which the bundles are about 8 μm tall and are separated by approximately 15 μm (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bullfrog saccular hair bundles.

claim: In the rat's cochlea, the distance between the row of inner hair cells and the first row of outer hair cells is only 10 μm.
source: In the rat's cochlea, however, the distance between the row of inner hair cells and the first row of outer hair cells is only 10 μm, and successive rows of outer hair cells are still more closely apposed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rat cochlear anatomy.

claim: Successive rows of outer hair cells in the rat's cochlea are still more closely apposed than inner and outer hair cells.
source: In the rat's cochlea, however, the distance between the row of inner hair cells and the first row of outer hair cells is only 10 μm, and successive rows of outer hair cells are still more closely apposed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rat cochlear anatomy.

claim: Introducing the optical fiber beneath the objective lens at an angle of 20° from the horizontal allowed the tip to approach a target hair bundle closely enough to ensure efficient stimulation.
source: After securing the end of a tapered optical fiber in a stable holder, we found that introducing it beneath the objective lens at an angle of 20° from the horizontal allowed the tip to approach a target hair bundle closely enough—typically about 7 μm—to ensure efficient stimulation, and at the same time positioned the tip far enough above other bundles to avoid damaging them (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup developed by the authors.

claim: The optical fiber tip was typically positioned about 7 μm from the target hair bundle.
source: After securing the end of a tapered optical fiber in a stable holder, we found that introducing it beneath the objective lens at an angle of 20° from the horizontal allowed the tip to approach a target hair bundle closely enough—typically about 7 μm—to ensure efficient stimulation, and at the same time positioned the tip far enough above other bundles to avoid damaging them (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The 20° angle positioned the fiber tip far enough above other bundles to avoid damaging them.
source: After securing the end of a tapered optical fiber in a stable holder, we found that introducing it beneath the objective lens at an angle of 20° from the horizontal allowed the tip to approach a target hair bundle closely enough—typically about 7 μm—to ensure efficient stimulation, and at the same time positioned the tip far enough above other bundles to avoid damaging them (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Photonic force from a tapered optical fiber could move glass rods of stiffness comparable to that of a hair bundle.
source: Before engaging in experiments with hair bundles, we conducted control experiments to confirm that photonic force from a tapered optical fiber could move an object of stiffness comparable to that of a bundle.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments described in Appendix 1.

claim: Irradiation of glass rods elicited a prompt movement in the expected direction.
source: In both cases, we found that irradiation elicited a prompt movement in the expected direction (see Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: The authors stimulated 40 hair bundles of the bullfrog's sacculus with radiation pressure toward their tall edges.
source: We stimulated 40 hair bundles of the bullfrog's sacculus so that radiation pressure would push them toward their tall edges—the positive direction—and reliably elicited the expected movements (see Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of experiments performed.

claim: Radiation pressure reliably elicited the expected movements in bullfrog hair bundles.
source: We stimulated 40 hair bundles of the bullfrog's sacculus so that radiation pressure would push them toward their tall edges—the positive direction—and reliably elicited the expected movements (see Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The responses of bullfrog hair bundles reached displacements as great as 500 nm.
source: The responses, which reached displacements as great as 500 nm, encompassed the range of complex trajectories reported in the literature (Benser et al., 1996; Tobin et al., 2019; Ricci et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to literature.

claim: The responses encompassed the range of complex trajectories reported in the literature.
source: The responses, which reached displacements as great as 500 nm, encompassed the range of complex trajectories reported in the literature (Benser et al., 1996; Tobin et al., 2019; Ricci et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited literature.

claim: More compliant hair bundles displayed relatively slow movements in the direction of the photonic force, a signature of the adaptation process.
source: The more compliant hair bundles—those displaying initial deflections exceeding about 150 nm—displayed relatively slow movements in the direction of the photonic force, a signature of the timescale of the adaptation process that allows hair cells to reset their operating points and thus detect successive stimuli (Figure 2A, gray arrows) (Howard and Hudspeth, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2A and citation to previous work on adaptation.

claim: The adaptation process allows hair cells to reset their operating points and detect successive stimuli.
source: The more compliant hair bundles—those displaying initial deflections exceeding about 150 nm—displayed relatively slow movements in the direction of the photonic force, a signature of the timescale of the adaptation process that allows hair cells to reset their operating points and thus detect successive stimuli (Figure 2A, gray arrows) (Howard and Hudspeth, 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge about adaptation, supported by citation.

claim: The twitch is a faster rebound of the hair bundle in a direction opposite to that of the stimulus.
source: The twitch, a faster rebound of the hair bundle in a direction opposite to that of the stimulus, is another manifestation of the adaptation process that occurs instead in response to smaller movements of the hair bundle and whose magnitude decreases for larger deflections (Benser et al., 1996; Ricci et al., 2000; Cheung and Corey, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the twitch response, supported by citations.

claim: The twitch is another manifestation of the adaptation process that occurs in response to smaller movements of the hair bundle.
source: The twitch, a faster rebound of the hair bundle in a direction opposite to that of the stimulus, is another manifestation of the adaptation process that occurs instead in response to smaller movements of the hair bundle and whose magnitude decreases for larger deflections (Benser et al., 1996; Ricci et al., 2000; Cheung and Corey, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the twitch response, supported by citations.

claim: The magnitude of the twitch decreases for larger deflections.
source: The twitch, a faster rebound of the hair bundle in a direction opposite to that of the stimulus, is another manifestation of the adaptation process that occurs instead in response to smaller movements of the hair bundle and whose magnitude decreases for larger deflections (Benser et al., 1996; Ricci et al., 2000; Cheung and Corey, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the twitch response, supported by citations.

claim: The twitch was observed in stiffer bundles with deflections of about 50 nm.
source: The twitch was indeed observed in stiffer bundles with deflections of about 50 nm (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Photonic force is an effective means of stimulating hair bundles.
source: These results indicate that photonic force is an effective means of stimulating hair bundles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results presented.

claim: Stereocilia are densely filled with parallel actin filaments that exhibit pronounced birefringence.
source: Because stereocilia are densely filled with parallel actin filaments that exhibit pronounced birefringence (Katoh et al., 1999), we inquired how this property affected the movement of the bullfrog's hair bundles upon photonic-force stimulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The light-induced deflection of hair bundles declined monotonically to an angle of 40°-50° as polarization was rotated, but remained roughly constant thereafter.
source: The light-induced deflection declined monotonically to an angle of 40°-50°, but remained roughly constant thereafter (see Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The response did not decline as the cosine of the angle, likely because stereocilia are not parallel, evenly spaced cylinders but a more complex array.
source: That the response did not decline as the cosine of the angle likely reflected the fact that stereocilia are not parallel, evenly spaced cylinders but rather a more complex array with varying tilts and separations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and knowledge of stereociliary structure.

claim: The beam's polarization was held parallel with the hair bundles' long axes in subsequent experiments.
source: This result nonetheless emphasized the importance of attending to the beam's polarization, which was held parallel with the hair bundles' long axes in subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The authors applied photonic stimuli to the hair bundles of both inner and outer hair cells from the cochleas of young rats.
source: We applied photonic stimuli to the hair bundles of both inner and outer hair cells from the cochleas of young rats.
evidence: This is a description of experiments performed.

claim: Mammalian hair bundles are stiffer than their amphibian counterparts.
source: Consistent with previous evidence that mammalian hair bundles are stiffer than their amphibian counterparts (Tobin et al., 2019), the recorded amplitudes of deflection were typically smaller (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data.

claim: The recorded amplitudes of deflection in rat hair bundles were typically smaller than in bullfrog hair bundles.
source: Consistent with previous evidence that mammalian hair bundles are stiffer than their amphibian counterparts (Tobin et al., 2019), the recorded amplitudes of deflection were typically smaller (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The time constants for the initial displacements of rat hair bundles were a few hundred microseconds.
source: The time constants for the initial displacements were again a few hundred microseconds.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The authors applied positive stimuli to 22 outer hair cells from three preparations.
source: To characterize the efficacy of photonic stimulation for rat hair bundles, we applied positive stimuli to 22 outer hair cells from three preparations.
evidence: This is a description of experiments performed.

claim: The authors deflected 13 outer hair cell bundles with amplitudes varying from 25 nm to 35 nm.
source: We deflected 13 hair bundles with amplitudes varying from 25 nm to 35 nm.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: The authors deflected seven of nine bundles from inner hair cells.
source: We also deflected seven of nine bundles from inner hair cells; the response amplitudes varied from 100 nm to 75 nm and the trajectories resembled those from the frog.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: The response amplitudes of inner hair cell bundles varied from 100 nm to 75 nm.
source: We also deflected seven of nine bundles from inner hair cells; the response amplitudes varied from 100 nm to 75 nm and the trajectories resembled those from the frog.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: The trajectories of inner hair cell bundle responses resembled those from the frog.
source: We also deflected seven of nine bundles from inner hair cells; the response amplitudes varied from 100 nm to 75 nm and the trajectories resembled those from the frog.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: The fiber's power delivered onto a hair bundle can be modulated by changing the laser's power at the source.
source: The fiber's power delivered onto a hair bundle can be modulated by changing the laser's power at the source.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental capability.

claim: By combining analog and digital signals to drive the laser's output, the authors were able to stimulate hair bundles with an assortment of stimuli.
source: By combining analog and digital signals to drive the laser's output, we were able to stimulate hair bundles with an assortment of stimuli: sine waves, frequency sweeps, step pulses of various magnitudes, and continuously ascending and descending ramps (see Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The responses of bullfrog's hair bundles followed sinusoidal frequency sweeps at frequencies up to 2 kHz.
source: The responses of bullfrog's hair bundles followed sinusoidal frequency sweeps at frequencies up to 2 kHz (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The upper boundary in the stimulus frequency was set by the ability of the hair bundle to follow, rather than by the limitations of the stimulation method.
source: In this case the upper boundary in the stimulus frequency was set by the ability of the hair bundle to follow, rather than by the limitations of the stimulation method.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: A hair bundle from the frog can move in the positive direction in response to laser irradiation of the cellular apex from any direction as a result of localized heat generation.
source: As a result of localized heat generation, a hair bundle from the frog can move in the positive direction in response to laser irradiation of the cellular apex from any direction (Azimzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The photothermal effect also occurs in hair bundles of the rat.
source: We found that this phenomenon also occurs in hair bundles of the rat (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The photothermal effect requires intact tip links.
source: To separate this photothermal effect from that of photonic force, we took advantage of the fact that the former requires intact tip links.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the photothermal effect.

claim: When tip links were disrupted with BAPTA to abolish the photothermal effect, both positive and negative stimuli evoked rapid movements in the direction of light propagation.
source: When we disrupted the tip links with BAPTA to abolish the photothermal effect, we observed that both positive and negative stimuli evoked rapid movements in the direction of light propagation (see Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Hair bundles stimulated along a direction perpendicular to their axis of symmetry moved in the direction of photon flux.
source: We also stimulated hair bundles along a direction perpendicular to their axis of symmetry and again found that they moved in the direction of photon flux (see Appendix 1—figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5C.

claim: Bundle motion upon photonic stimulation can occur in the absence of a photothermal effect.
source: These results indicate that bundle motion upon photonic stimulation can occur in the absence of a photothermal effect: bundle movements stem solely from optical radiation force.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results with BAPTA treatment.

claim: Bundle movements stem solely from optical radiation force when the photothermal effect is abolished.
source: These results indicate that bundle motion upon photonic stimulation can occur in the absence of a photothermal effect: bundle movements stem solely from optical radiation force.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results with BAPTA treatment.

claim: In a frog's hair cell, the photothermal effect apparently results from light absorption by the mitochondria that accumulate around the cuticular plate at the cell's apical surface.
source: In a frog's hair cell, the photothermal effect apparently results from light absorption by the mitochondria that accumulate around the cuticular plate at the cell's apical surface (Azimzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mammalian outer hair cells, mitochondria are concentrated at the lateral plasma membrane.
source: Because in mammalian outer hair cells mitochondria are instead concentrated at the lateral plasma membrane (Fuchs, 2010), it was possible to isolate the photothermal effect by directing light well below the apical cell surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: It was possible to isolate the photothermal effect in mammalian outer hair cells by directing light well below the apical cell surface.
source: Because in mammalian outer hair cells mitochondria are instead concentrated at the lateral plasma membrane (Fuchs, 2010), it was possible to isolate the photothermal effect by directing light well below the apical cell surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of mitochondria.

claim: The photothermal movement was relatively slow with a time constant of 2 ms, about ten times that of movements owing to photonic force.
source: Note that the photothermal movement was relatively slow: its time constant of 2 ms was about ten times that of the movements owing to photonic force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the two types of movements.

claim: It was possible to avert the photothermal effect by irradiating a mammalian hair bundle with intact tip links while avoiding irradiation of the cell body.
source: Conversely, it was possible to avert the photothermal effect by irradiating a mammalian hair bundle with intact tip links while avoiding irradiation of the cell body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of mitochondria and the mechanism of the photothermal effect.

claim: The hair bundles of healthy hair cells from the bullfrog can oscillate back-and-forth even in the absence of external stimulation.
source: The hair bundles of healthy hair cells from the bullfrog can oscillate back-and-forth even in the absence of external stimulation (Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Spontaneous oscillations are a manifestation of the active process that hair cells employ to amplify mechanical stimuli by counteracting viscous damping.
source: These spontaneous oscillations are a manifestation of the active process that these cells employ to amplify mechanical stimuli by counteracting viscous damping.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the active process in hair cells.

claim: The presence of spontaneous oscillations requires a fully functional transduction apparatus.
source: The presence of spontaneous oscillations, which require a fully functional transduction apparatus, offers a means of assessing the viability of hair cells and the preservation of mechanotransduction following exposure to laser irradiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spontaneous oscillations.

claim: The authors compared the spontaneous oscillations of six hair cells before and after subjecting them to 25 pulses of light.
source: We compared the spontaneous oscillations of six hair cells before and after subjecting them to 25 pulses of light.
evidence: This is a description of experiments performed.

claim: Even at laser powers sufficient to deflect hair bundles over their entire physiological range of motion, the amplitudes and frequencies of the bundles' oscillation were unaffected by laser irradiation.
source: Even at laser powers sufficient to deflect hair bundles over their entire physiological range of motion, the amplitudes and frequencies of the bundles' oscillation were unaffected by laser irradiation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mechanotransduction apparatus was not damaged by the photonic stimulation method.
source: This experiment demonstrates that the mechanotransduction apparatus was not damaged by our stimulation method.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the preservation of spontaneous oscillations.

claim: The authors used tapered optical fibers to apply both rapid and prolonged forces to individual hair bundles.
source: We have used tapered optical fibers to apply both rapid and prolonged forces to individual hair bundles.
evidence: This is a summary of the work presented.

claim: The tip of each tapered fiber was small enough to be positioned near a hair bundle.
source: The tip of each tapered fiber was small enough to be positioned near a hair bundle, and the ball lens at its tip restricted the divergence of the emitted light beam.
evidence: This is a description of the fabricated fibers.

claim: The ball lens at the fiber's tip restricted the divergence of the emitted light beam.
source: The tip of each tapered fiber was small enough to be positioned near a hair bundle, and the ball lens at its tip restricted the divergence of the emitted light beam.
evidence: This is a description of the fabricated fibers.

claim: Irradiation could be confined to a single bundle.
source: Irradiation could be confined to a single bundle, whereupon the uniform illumination of all the stereocilia implied that each experienced a similar photonic force.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental capability.

claim: The uniform illumination of all the stereocilia implied that each experienced a similar photonic force.
source: Irradiation could be confined to a single bundle, whereupon the uniform illumination of all the stereocilia implied that each experienced a similar photonic force.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uniform illumination.

claim: It was possible to irradiate only a portion of a bundle.
source: It was also possible to irradiate only a portion of a bundle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental capability.

claim: Control experiments indicated that even extensive irradiation of the magnitude necessary to evoke large displacements did not harm the hair bundles.
source: Our control experiments indicated that even extensive irradiation of the magnitude necessary to evoke large displacements did not harm the hair bundles.
evidence: This is supported by the spontaneous oscillation experiments.

claim: Fabrication of a tapered optical fiber requires specialized equipment and a safe environment for the use of etching solution.
source: Although a routine procedure after the assembly of the necessary facilities, fabrication of a tapered optical fiber requires specialized equipment and a safe environment for the use of etching solution.
evidence: This is a description of the requirements for the method.

claim: The force exerted by photonic stimulation is not easily measured.
source: A second issue is calibration: unlike the force delivered by a flexible fiber, which can be calibrated through the fiber's Brownian motion, the force exerted by photonic stimulation is not easily measured.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the method.

claim: The force can be estimated by the use of targets whose stiffness has been independently determined.
source: The force can nonetheless be estimated by the use of targets whose stiffness has been independently determined, especially glass fibers such as those used in this study, or passive hair bundles including those subjected to chemical fixation.
evidence: This is a description of a method for force estimation.

claim: Stimulation by photonic force is rapid.
source: First, stimulation is rapid: in the present study, the rise time of mechanical responses was set by a hair bundle's stiffness and drag coefficient, without any effect of the drag on a stimulus fiber or the inertia of a piezoelectric actuator.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing rapid responses.

claim: In the present study, the rise time of mechanical responses was set by a hair bundle's stiffness and drag coefficient, without any effect of the drag on a stimulus fiber or the inertia of a piezoelectric actuator.
source: First, stimulation is rapid: in the present study, the rise time of mechanical responses was set by a hair bundle's stiffness and drag coefficient, without any effect of the drag on a stimulus fiber or the inertia of a piezoelectric actuator.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental setup and results.

claim: Stimulation could be made still more rapid by a process analogous to 'supercharging' in a voltage-clamp system.
source: Second, stimulation could be made still more rapid by a process analogous to 'supercharging' in a voltage-clamp system (Armstrong and Chow, 1987): transient irradiation with a very bright light could be used to deflect a bundle to a desired position, after which a steady force would be applied by weaker illumination during the measurement of a response.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential improvement to the method, supported by analogy to voltage-clamp.

claim: Because illumination can be switched off, there is no possibility of an ill-defined steady-state offset in bundle position owing to mispositioning of a fiber or leakage from a fluid jet.
source: Because illumination can be switched off, a third virtue is that there is no possibility of an ill-defined steady-state offset in bundle position owing to mispositioning of a fiber or leakage from a fluid jet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the photonic stimulation method.

claim: The uniform illumination of the stereocilia in a bundle offers an advantage, especially for mammalian hair bundles that exhibit relatively poor lateral coupling between stereocilia.
source: The uniform illumination of the stereocilia in a bundle offers a fourth advantage, especially for mammalian hair bundles that exhibit relatively poor lateral coupling between stereocilia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the method and mammalian hair bundles.

claim: Photonic stimulation can be used in spaces too restricted to admit a flexible fiber or fluid jet.
source: And finally, photonic stimulation can be used in spaces too restricted to admit a flexible fiber or fluid jet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small size of the tapered fiber tip.

claim: It should be possible to stimulate one or several hair bundles in preparations such as a hemicochlea or an isolated cochlear segment.
source: In particular, it should be possible to stimulate one or several hair bundles in preparations such as a hemicochlea (He et al., 2004) or an isolated cochlear segment (Chan and Hudspeth, 2005a; Chan and Hudspeth, 2005b).
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications, supported by citations to relevant preparations.

claim: Each absorbed photon imparts all of its original momentum to the absorbing object.
source: Each absorbed photon imparts all of its original momentum to the absorbing object and thereby provides an impulsive force.
evidence: This is established knowledge from physics.

claim: A reflected photon delivers twice the momentum provided by an absorbed one.
source: A reflected photon delivers twice the momentum provided by an absorbed one, whereas a refracted photon imparts momentum dependent on the angle of refraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge from physics.

claim: A refracted photon imparts momentum dependent on the angle of refraction.
source: A reflected photon delivers twice the momentum provided by an absorbed one, whereas a refracted photon imparts momentum dependent on the angle of refraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge from physics.

claim: Reflection sets the upper limit of the force that might be delivered to a hair bundle by a particular beam of light.
source: Because reflection sets the upper limit of the force that might be delivered to a hair bundle by a particular beam of light, we begin our analysis by treating the bundle as a perfect reflector.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of photonic force.

claim: For 10 mW of laser power that impinges normal to the surface of a perfect reflector in physiological solution, approximately 80 pN of force is generated.
source: Therefore, in the purely reflective case, using Equation 3, we estimate that 10 mW of laser power that impinges normal to the surface of the reflector generates approximately 80 pN of force.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the physics of radiation pressure.

claim: The upper limit of force from reflection is not achievable because stereocilia are not perfect mirrors.
source: However, this upper limit of the force is not achievable because stereocilia are not perfect mirrors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optical properties of stereocilia.

claim: The actual force experienced by a hair bundle depends on the difference of the refractive indices between the solution and the stereocilia.
source: The actual force experienced by a hair bundle depends on the difference of the refractive indices between the solution and the stereocilia, a larger difference indicating more reflected light and larger force.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of reflection and refraction.

claim: The refractive index of stereocilia is expected to be approximately 1.4.
source: We expect the refractive index of the stereocilium to be approximately 1.4.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the Gladstone-Dale relation and protein concentration.

claim: The photonic force generated from simple reflection is about 0.45 pN, a force unable to move a hair bundle appreciably.
source: The photonic force generated from reflection is therefore about 0.45 pN, a force unable to move a hair bundle appreciably.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the reflected power.

claim: A simple model of reflection must be rejected in favor of an understanding based on the reflective properties of curved surfaces.
source: We must therefore reject a simple model of reflection and seek an understanding based on the reflective properties of curved surfaces.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inadequacy of the simple reflection model.

claim: The reflectivity is significantly higher for a curved object than for a planar one.
source: The reflectivity, or fraction of backscattered light, is significantly higher for a curved object than for a planar one (Ashkin, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: For a cylinder with an aspect ratio of 15, similar to that of a stereocilium, the reflectivity is about 3.5 times that of a sphere of equal volume.
source: However, it has been shown that for a cylinder with an aspect ratio of 15, similar to that of a stereocilium of length 8 μm and diameter 0.5 μm, the reflectivity is about 3.5 times that of a sphere of equal volume (Gordon, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stereocilia likely form a grating that exhibits complex interference effects because they are closely spaced in a regular geometric array.
source: Moreover, because stereocilia are closely spaced in a regular geometric array, they likely form a grating that exhibits complex interference effects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the geometry of stereocilia.

claim: The qualitative description emphasizes the importance of stereociliary curvature in providing exceptionally high reflection and unexpectedly great forces on stereocilia.
source: Nonetheless, even the qualitative description offered above emphasizes the importance of stereociliary curvature in providing exceptionally high reflection and unexpectedly great forces on stereocilia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of light interaction with cylindrical stereocilia.

claim: It is possible to estimate the photonic force from the stiffness of the moving hair bundle.
source: It is possible to estimate the photonic force that elicited a given hair-cell response from the stiffness of the moving hair bundle.
evidence: This is a description of a method for force estimation.

claim: A 50 ms pulse of photonic pressure at 12.5 mW output power elicited a 20 nm deflection of a bullfrog hair bundle whose stiffness was 1.8 ± 0.2 mN•m–1.
source: A 50 ms pulse of photonic pressure at 12.5 mW output power elicited a 20 nm deflection of the hair bundle, whose stiffness was subsequently measured to be 1.8 ± 0.2 mN•m–1 (mean ± SEM)—a relatively stiff hair bundle.
evidence: This is experimental data from a specific measurement.

claim: Approximately 40 pN was delivered to the hair bundle by radiation pressure in the empirical estimation.
source: This allowed us to estimate that approximately 40 pN was delivered to the hair bundle by radiation pressure.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured stiffness and displacement.

claim: Turner's wet chemical etching with hydrofluoric acid was used to create tapered optical fibers.
source: We created tapered optical fibers by Turner's wet chemical etching with hydrofluoric acid (André et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication method, supported by citation.

claim: With the etching method, a fiber can be shaped in about 1.5 hr in any laboratory with a fume hood and few tools.
source: With this method, a fiber can be shaped in about 1.5 hr in any laboratory with a fume hood and few tools.
evidence: This is a description of the practical aspects of the fabrication method.

claim: The fluorescence signal from laser-irradiated hair bundles showed no visible difference with respect to that of unscathed cells in FM1-43 uptake experiments.
source: The fluorescence signal from laser-irradiated hair bundles showed no visible difference with respect to that of the unscathed cells, whereas mechanically damaged bundles were visibly dimmer.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Mechanically damaged bundles were visibly dimmer in FM1-43 uptake experiments.
source: The fluorescence signal from laser-irradiated hair bundles showed no visible difference with respect to that of the unscathed cells, whereas mechanically damaged bundles were visibly dimmer.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The diminished fluorescence in mechanically damaged bundles likely resulted from breakage of the tip links that reduced the opening of the mechanotransduction channels.
source: This diminished fluorescence likely resulted from breakage of the tip links that reduced the opening of the mechanotransduction channels, thereby limiting the intake of the dye.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of FM1-43 uptake.
